content: The choice of vaccination delivery strategies, whether school-based or community-based, should be determined by factors such as the age-specific incidence of the disease, the presence of high-risk subgroups, and school enrollment rates. This decision should be made by the respective countries. Additionally, the selection of the Vi or Ty21a typhoid vaccine depends on the capacity of the local immunization program and other logistical and cultural considerations. Given the epidemic potential of typhoid fever and the observed effectiveness of vaccination in controlling outbreaks, typhoid fever vaccination is also recommended for outbreak management. Countries where yellow fever is endemic should incorporate the yellow fever vaccine into their routine immunization programs, administering it to children aged 9–12 months alongside the measles vaccine. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-quality evidence. HIV-exposed infants and children, as well as young adults with HIV, should receive all vaccines included in the national immunization schedules. Those with severe immunosuppression may face higher risks of complications from live vaccines. Inactivated vaccines are more effective in individuals receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) and those without immunosuppression, but they are safe and can be used with some efficacy in all groups. Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for all infants from birth until six months of age. Mothers should receive counseling and support for exclusive breastfeeding during each postnatal contact, and breastfeeding progress should be assessed regularly. Facilities providing maternity and newborn care should implement the Ten Steps to Successful Breastfeeding, which include having a written breastfeeding policy, training healthcare staff, informing pregnant women about breastfeeding benefits, initiating breastfeeding within 30 minutes of birth, and avoiding the use of artificial teats or pacifiers. In rare cases where breastfeeding is not possible due to maternal or infant conditions, breast-milk substitutes may be required. However, nearly all women are capable of breastfeeding. Neonatal vitamin A supplementation (within the first 28 days of life) is not recommended as a public health intervention to reduce infant morbidity and mortality. Similarly, vitamin A supplementation for infants aged 1–5 months is not recommended. However, in settings where vitamin A deficiency is a public health problem, supplementation is recommended for children aged 6–59 months to reduce morbidity and mortality. Daily iron supplementation is recommended for infants and young children aged 6–23 months and preschool-aged children aged 24–59 months in areas with high anemia prevalence. For school-aged children (60 months and older) in such settings, daily iron supplementation is also recommended to prevent iron deficiency and anemia. In populations with high anemia prevalence, point-of-use fortification of complementary foods with iron-containing micronutrient powders is recommended for children aged 6–23 months and 2–12 years to improve iron status and reduce anemia. Infants born to mothers with suspected or confirmed Zika virus infection should be fed according to standard infant feeding guidelines, including exclusive breastfeeding for six months and continued breastfeeding up to two years or beyond. In areas of moderate-to-high malaria transmission in Africa, intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) is recommended for infants during the second and third rounds of diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis (DTP) vaccination and measles vaccination. In areas with highly seasonal malaria transmission in sub-Saharan Africa, seasonal malaria chemoprevention with monthly amodiaquine and SP is recommended for children under six years during the transmission season. In settings with high tuberculosis (TB) prevalence, a single dose of the BCG vaccine should be given to all infants. However, BCG vaccination is not recommended for HIV-infected children. For infants born to HIV-positive mothers with unknown HIV status, BCG vaccination should be considered based on local factors. Household and close contacts of TB cases should be evaluated for active TB, with priority given to children under five years, those with immunocompromising conditions, and contacts of multidrug-resistant TB cases. Children under five years who are close contacts of TB cases and do not have active TB should receive six months of isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT). In settings with high HIV prevalence, all household and close contacts of TB cases should be counseled and tested for HIV. In low HIV prevalence settings, contacts with TB symptoms may be offered HIV testing as part of their clinical evaluation. Mothers living with HIV should exclusively breastfeed for the first six months and continue breastfeeding for at least 12 months, with ART adherence support. If breastfeeding is stopped, it should be done gradually over one month, and replacement feeding should meet specific safety and adequacy criteria. For HIV-exposed infants at high risk of acquiring HIV, dual prophylaxis with AZT and NVP is recommended for the first six weeks of life. Breastfed infants at high risk should continue prophylaxis for an additional six weeks. Mothers living with HIV may consider expressing and heat-treating breast milk as an interim feeding strategy in specific circumstances, such as when the infant is unable to breastfeed or when ART is temporarily unavailable. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for all HIV-infected infants, children, and adolescents, particularly those under five years or with advanced HIV disease. In malaria-endemic areas, co-trimoxazole is also effective in preventing severe bacterial infections.
